name: Poha
cuisine: Maharashtrian (Mumbai-style kanda poha), also eaten across Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat

ingredients.name: Groundnut oil (or any neutral cooking oil)
Onion (kanda/pyaz)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ medium onion, finely chopped (about ⅓ cup)

equipment: Kadai or wide frying pan with a lid
Measuring spoons and a measuring cup (a regular tea cup and teaspoons work as a stand-in)

steps.title: Measure the poha
steps.text: Put 60 g (¾ cup) thick poha into the colander.
steps.tip: Pick out any husk or small stones you see.
steps.visualCue: The flakes are whole, flat and off-white, not broken into powder.
steps.cameraCheck: The colander with ¾ cup of dry poha
steps.videoShot: The poha pouring from the cup into the colander.
steps.watchOut: Thin (patla) poha or a lot of broken dust at the bottom of the pack, which turns to paste when rinsed; if that is all you have, rinse for only 10 seconds.

steps.title: Rinse the poha
steps.text: Hold the colander under running tap water and gently turn the flakes with your fingers so all of them get wet.
steps.tip: Do not soak the poha in a bowl of water. Several sources name this as the main reason poha turns mushy.
steps.visualCue: Every flake looks wet and a shade brighter, and the water running off is mostly clear.
steps.cameraCheck: The wet poha in the colander
steps.videoShot: Water running over the poha while fingers turn it.
steps.watchOut: Rinsing too long or soaking in a bowl, which makes the flakes slimy and the dish mushy; stop at 30 seconds, the flakes finish softening while they rest.

steps.title: Drain the poha
steps.text: Shake the colander 2–3 times and leave it over a bowl to drain.
steps.visualCue: No water is dripping out any more, and the flakes look damp, not sitting in water.
steps.cameraCheck: The colander resting over the bowl
steps.videoShot: The colander being shaken and set down.
steps.watchOut: Leaving it standing in water, which keeps soaking it; if the bottom looks wet, shake again and tilt the colander.

steps.title: Season and rest the poha
steps.text: Sprinkle 1.5 g (¼ tsp) salt, 2 g (½ tsp) sugar and 0.5 g (⅛ tsp) turmeric over the damp poha. Toss gently with your fingertips, then leave it to rest.
steps.tip: Adding the turmeric now, not in the pan, gives an even colour without stirring the poha too much later.
steps.visualCue: The flakes turn an even pale yellow and slowly turn soft.
steps.cameraCheck: The yellow poha in the colander
steps.videoShot: The spices sprinkling over the poha, then a gentle toss.
steps.watchOut: Patchy colour from turmeric lumps, so toss until no white flakes or yellow clumps remain. Pressing or squeezing the flakes breaks them.

steps.title: Chop the onion
steps.text: Finely chop 60 g (½ medium) onion.
steps.visualCue: Small, even pieces about the size of a grain of rice or a lentil.
steps.cameraCheck: ⅓ cup of chopped onion on the board
steps.videoShot: The knife chopping the onion into small dice.
steps.watchOut: Big chunks, which stay crunchy and raw-tasting in the quick cook; cut them again smaller.

steps.title: Chop the chilli
steps.text: Slit 1 green chilli (5 g) and cut it into small pieces.
steps.tip: Want it less hot? Remove the seeds first.
steps.visualCue: Thin rings or small bits
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped chilli on the board
steps.videoShot: The knife cutting the chilli.
steps.watchOut: Touching your eyes after cutting chilli, which stings; wash your hands with soap straight away.

steps.title: Prepare the herbs
steps.text: Wash 6–8 curry leaves and pat them dry. Chop 5 g (1 tbsp) coriander leaves.
steps.visualCue: The curry leaves are dry and glossy with no water drops.
steps.cameraCheck: The curry leaves and chopped coriander side by side
steps.videoShot: The coriander being chopped.
steps.watchOut: Wet curry leaves, which splutter hard in hot oil; pat them dry with a cloth or paper.

steps.title: Cut the lemon
steps.text: Cut ¼ of a lemon and keep it ready.
steps.visualCue: A juicy wedge
steps.cameraCheck: The lemon wedge
steps.videoShot: The knife cutting the lemon wedge.
steps.watchOut: Seeds falling into the poha later; pick them out of the wedge now.

steps.title: Heat the oil
steps.text: Put the kadai on medium heat and add 10 ml (2 tsp) oil.
steps.visualCue: The oil shimmers and flows easily when you tilt the pan.
steps.cameraCheck: The kadai with oil
steps.videoShot: The oil swirling in the pan.
steps.watchOut: Smoking oil, which burns the spices and tastes bitter; if it smokes, switch off the heat for 20 seconds before going on.

steps.title: Fry the peanuts
steps.text: Add 10 g (1 tbsp) peanuts and stir.
steps.tip: Take them out with a spoon and set aside if you want them extra crunchy. Otherwise leave them in.
steps.visualCue: The skins darken a little, the peanuts smell nutty and turn crunchy.
steps.cameraCheck: Golden peanuts in the pan
steps.videoShot: The peanuts being stirred in the oil.
steps.watchOut: Peanuts that turn dark brown, which taste bitter; take them out as soon as they smell roasted. Soft peanuts need another 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the mustard seeds
steps.text: Add 1 g (¼ tsp) mustard seeds.
steps.visualCue: The seeds crackle and pop within about 10–20 seconds.
steps.cameraCheck: Popping seeds in the pan
steps.videoShot: The mustard seeds spluttering.
steps.watchOut: Seeds that do not pop because the oil is not hot enough, which taste raw; wait a few more seconds. Seeds that turn grey and bitter are burnt, so lower the heat.

steps.title: Add the cumin
steps.text: Add 0.5 g (⅛ tsp) cumin seeds (optional).
steps.visualCue: The cumin sizzles and darkens slightly, with a toasty smell.
steps.cameraCheck: The pan
steps.videoShot: The cumin sizzling.
steps.watchOut: Black, smoky cumin, which tastes bitter; go straight to the next step as soon as it sizzles.

steps.title: Add the curry leaves and chilli
steps.text: Add the curry leaves and green chilli.
steps.tip: Stand back. Wet leaves splutter hard.
steps.visualCue: A loud splutter, then the leaves turn crisp and glossy and smell strong.
steps.cameraCheck: The leaves and chilli in the oil
steps.videoShot: The leaves hitting the oil.
steps.watchOut: Hot oil splashing when the leaves go in; stand back and tilt the lid towards you as a shield.

steps.title: Sauté the onion
steps.text: Add the chopped onion and stir.
steps.visualCue: The onion turns soft and translucent, and smells sweet, not browned.
steps.cameraCheck: The soft onions in the pan
steps.videoShot: The onions being stirred.
steps.watchOut: Browning, which adds a bitter, roasted taste unlike classic kanda poha; lower the heat and sprinkle a spoon of water if the edges brown.

steps.title: Check the poha
steps.text: Press a flake between your fingers.
steps.visualCue: It squashes easily but holds its shape and is not pasty. If it still feels hard, sprinkle 1 tbsp water over it and wait 2 min.
steps.cameraCheck: A flake pressed between your fingers
steps.videoShot: Fingers pressing a flake.
steps.watchOut: A hard centre that stays crunchy in the finished dish, or a sticky paste that means it was over-wet; hard flakes can be rescued with a sprinkle of water, but over-wet poha cannot, so go gently next time.

steps.title: Add the poha
steps.text: Turn the heat to low and add the rested poha to the pan.
steps.visualCue: A yellow pile sitting over the onions
steps.cameraCheck: The pan with the poha added
steps.videoShot: The poha sliding into the pan.
steps.watchOut: Dropping it onto high heat, which dries and sticks the flakes; keep the flame low.

steps.title: Mix the poha
steps.text: Fold gently from the bottom with the spatula until the onions and peanuts spread through it.
steps.tip: Lift and fold. Do not press or mash.
steps.visualCue: Even yellow colour with no white patches, and the flakes are still separate.
steps.cameraCheck: The mixed poha
steps.videoShot: The spatula gently folding the poha.
steps.watchOut: Stirring hard, which breaks flakes into mush; lift and fold. Dry white patches mean the seasoning was uneven, so fold a little more.

steps.title: Steam the poha
steps.text: Cover with the lid and cook on low heat.
steps.visualCue: Steam on the inside of the lid, and the poha looks soft and fluffy when you open it.
steps.cameraCheck: The covered pan
steps.videoShot: The lid going on, then coming off to show steam.
steps.watchOut: Cooking longer than 2–3 minutes, which dries the poha and makes it hard to chew; if it already looks dry, sprinkle 1 tbsp water and cover for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the lemon
steps.text: Switch off the heat. Squeeze 5 ml (1 tsp) lemon juice over the poha.
steps.tip: Add lemon only after the heat is off.
steps.visualCue: A fresh, sharp lemon smell as the juice spreads over the top.
steps.cameraCheck: The lemon being squeezed over the pan
steps.videoShot: Lemon juice dripping over the poha.
steps.watchOut: Cooked lemon turning bitter, so always add it with the heat off. Too sour? Add a pinch of sugar.

steps.title: Add the coriander
steps.text: Scatter the chopped coriander over the poha and give it one last gentle fold.
steps.visualCue: Bright green flecks over yellow poha
steps.cameraCheck: The finished poha in the pan
steps.videoShot: The coriander falling onto the poha, then one fold.
steps.watchOut: Coriander turning dark and limp when added to a hot pan for too long; fold once and plate it.

steps.title: Plate the poha
steps.text: Spoon it onto a plate.
steps.visualCue: Fluffy, separate, yellow flakes with green herbs and brown peanuts
steps.cameraCheck: The served plate
steps.videoShot: A slow pan across the finished plate.
steps.watchOut: Letting it sit in the pan, where it keeps cooking and dries out; plate it right away and eat it warm.

reasons: the home version uses only 2 tsp oil, no deep frying and very little sugar (2 g). It gets some protein and healthy fat from the peanuts and vegetables from the onion and herbs, and has no cholesterol and only about 2.6 g saturated fat. It is still mostly refined carbohydrate with modest protein (about 8 g) and fibre (about 3 g), and the salt is about 30% of the daily limit. Restaurant versions usually use more oil, more sugar and a sev topping, which is deep-fried, so they are less healthy (est.).

researchRating.basis: poha is one of India's most-loved everyday breakfasts and a Mumbai staple, and recipe pages score very high (for example Indian Healthy Recipes: 5 stars from 301 votes, as seen in a search snippet). Points are deducted because many people see it as plain, everyday food, and its texture often goes wrong (mushy or dry), which is the most common warning in recipe tips.

storage: Can go in the fridge for up to 1 day in an airtight box (it dries out and hardens after that). Freezing is not recommended because the flakes go crumbly. To reheat, sprinkle 1–2 tsp water, cover, and heat on low in a pan for 2–3 min, or microwave covered for 45–60 sec. Add fresh lemon after reheating.
leftoverRemix: Poha cutlets. Mash the leftover poha with 1 boiled potato, 1 tbsp besan and a pinch of chaat masala. Shape into small patties and shallow-fry on a tawa with 1 tsp oil until crisp, about 3 min per side. Serve with green chutney. (Poha cutlets are a published dish, for example the Alamy photo caption "Veg Poha Cutlet or flattened Rice Patties" seen in search; the quantities here are FitPlate's.)
burnOff: about 5.6 km of running (390 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 7.8 km of brisk walking (about 1 hr 35 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).

navratri.reason: poha is rice-based and the recipe has onion; most vrat rule sets avoid grains and onion (common rule set assumed; sabudana khichdi is the usual vrat alternative)

ekadashi.reason: rice and rice products are commonly avoided on Ekadashi, and the recipe has onion (common rule set assumed; families differ)

jain.reason: drop the onion (60 g); no other root vegetable is in the recipe

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; light and quick, and fine for sehri if you add protein (curd, sprouts or paneer), since the plain dish has only about 8 g protein; sodium is about 600 mg, roughly 30% of the daily limit (section 5)

jain.reason: leave out the onion (60 g), a root vegetable under the Patch 05 rule; every other ingredient (poha, peanuts, curry leaves, chilli, turmeric powder, lemon, coriander) is allowed (see Jain variant)

vegan.reason: poha, peanuts, oil, vegetables and spices only; no dairy, ghee, honey or egg

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian recipe with no meat or egg

sattvik.reason: skip the onion; there is no garlic in the recipe (see Sattvik variant)

glutenFree.reason: rice flakes, no wheat, rava, maida or hing in the recipe; check that the poha pack is not processed alongside wheat

dairyFree.reason: no dairy in the recipe (serving with curd is optional and not part of it)

variants.reason: Main recipe already vegan (no dairy, ghee, honey or egg).
Main recipe already gluten-free (rice flakes; no wheat, rava, maida or hing).
